_about: Security acronyms for the Reference page (#acronyms): what each stands for and one plain sentence on what it means. Expansions follow the NIST CSRC Glossary and the acronym lists in CompTIA's exam objectives. One acronym can have several entries when it has several meanings (MAC, PAM, SOC, CSP). Kept in alphabetical order. tests/acronyms.test.mjs checks the shape.

source.title: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary

acronyms.plain: Logging in with two kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code from your phone.
Proving who you are, deciding what you may do, and recording what you did.
A list of rules on a file, router or firewall saying who or what is allowed or blocked.
The standard symmetric cipher (one shared key) used to encrypt Wi-Fi, disks and web traffic.
The expected cost of a risk per year: single loss expectancy (SLE) times annualized rate of occurrence (ARO).
A skilled, well-funded attacker group that gets into a network and stays hidden there for a long time.
How many times a year a risk is expected to happen (0.5 means once every two years).
Finds the MAC address for an IP address on a local network. Forged ARP replies can redirect traffic.
Loads programs at random memory addresses so memory-corruption exploits are harder to pull off.

acronyms.full: Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge
acronyms.plain: MITRE's public catalog of how real attackers operate, from first access to stealing data.
How an organization keeps its most important work going during and after a disruption.
Fraud where an attacker uses or imitates a work email account to get staff to send money or data.
Works out which business functions matter most and how long each can be down.
Staff using their own phones or laptops for work, usually under a policy.
The servers and channels attackers use to send orders to, and receive data from, infected machines.
A trusted organization that checks identities and signs digital certificates.
Sits between users and cloud apps to see what is used and enforce security policy.
The three core goals of security: keep data secret, keep it correct, and keep it reachable.
The US government agency for cyber defense; it runs the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
Browser rules that decide which other websites may read responses from a site.
A certificate authority's published list of certificates it cancelled before they expired.
The team that handles security incidents for an organization or country.
A header that tells the browser which scripts and resources a page may load, limiting XSS.
A company that sells cloud computing, such as AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud.
The request, containing your public key and details, that you send to a CA to get a certificate.
Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request to a site that the user never meant to send.
The public ID system for known vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2021-44228.
Rates how severe a vulnerability is on a scale of 0.0 to 10.0.
A catalog of software weakness types, such as CWE-79 for cross-site scripting.
The owner of a file or resource decides who else may use it.
Many machines flood a target at once so real users can't reach it.
Automatically gives devices an IP address and other network settings when they join.
A signature on outgoing email that proves which domain sent it and that it wasn't changed.
Tools and rules that spot sensitive data and stop it leaving the organization.

acronyms.full: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance
acronyms.plain: A domain's published policy for mail that fails SPF and DKIM checks, plus where to send reports.
A separate network segment for public-facing servers, kept apart from the internal network (also called a screened subnet).
Turns names like example.com into IP addresses.
Signs DNS answers so a resolver can tell if they were forged.
Sends DNS lookups inside encrypted web traffic so others on the network can't read or change them.
An attack that makes a system or service unavailable to the people who should be able to use it.
The steps for restoring IT systems and data after a major outage or disaster.
A framework for login methods on Wi-Fi and wired networks, used with 802.1X.
Public-key cryptography that gets the same strength as RSA with much smaller keys.
Software on laptops and servers that watches for attacks and lets responders investigate and act.
The share of an asset's value lost in one incident, as a percentage.
FIRST's estimate of how likely a CVE is to be exploited in the next 30 days.
Encrypts a whole drive so a lost or stolen device's data can't be read.
Alerts when important system or application files change unexpectedly.

acronyms.full: Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams
acronyms.plain: A global group of incident response teams; it maintains CVSS and EPSS.
European Union law on how personal data must be collected, used and protected.
How an organization sets security rules, manages risk and proves it meets laws and standards.
An IDS that runs on one computer and watches its logs, files and activity.

acronyms.full: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
acronyms.plain: US law that includes rules for protecting patients' health information.
A hash mixed with a secret key, proving a message came from someone with the key and wasn't changed.
A tamper-resistant device that stores cryptographic keys and uses them without letting them out.
Web traffic encrypted with TLS, shown by the padlock in the browser.
Renting virtual servers, storage and networks from a cloud provider; you manage the rest.
Managing user accounts and what each one is allowed to access.
Computers that run physical processes in factories, power plants and water systems.
An app returns a record by its ID without checking that you are allowed to see it.
Watches network traffic or a system and raises alerts on attacks, without blocking them.
Evidence of an attack, such as a malicious IP address, domain or file hash.
Everyday devices with network connections, such as cameras, thermostats and smart plugs.
Like an IDS, but sits in the traffic path and can block attacks.
Encrypts and authenticates IP traffic; widely used for site-to-site VPNs.
The process of preparing for, detecting, containing and recovering from security incidents.
A signed token that carries login details between a web app and its APIs.
CISA's catalog of CVEs that attackers are known to have used; patch these first.
Queries directories of users, groups and devices, such as Active Directory.
The hardware address of a network card, used on the local network.
The system, not the owner, decides access using labels such as Secret or Top Secret.
A short tag made with a secret key that proves a message wasn't changed.
An old hash algorithm that is broken for security use; still seen as a file fingerprint.
Central control of company phones and tablets: settings, apps, encryption and remote wipe.
Logging in with two or more kinds of proof, such as a password plus a phone prompt or security key.
An attacker secretly sits between two parties to read or change their traffic (now often called an on-path attack).
An outside company paid to monitor and manage an organization's security.
The average time a system runs before it fails.
The average time it takes to fix a system and get it working again after a failure.
Checks a device's identity and health before letting it onto the network.
Lets many devices with private addresses share one public IP address.
A contract in which people agree to keep certain information confidential.
A firewall that also recognizes applications and users, often with intrusion prevention built in.

acronyms.full: National Institute of Standards and Technology
acronyms.plain: US agency that publishes security standards such as the Cybersecurity Framework and SP 800-53.
Keeps device clocks in sync; correct time matters for logs, certificates and logins.
NIST's database that adds severity scores and affected products to CVE entries.
Lets an app access your account on another service without being given your password.
Asks a certificate authority, in real time, whether a certificate has been revoked.
Information gathered from public sources such as websites, social media and public records.
Hardware and software that monitor and control physical equipment, as opposed to office IT.
A code that works for a single login or a short time, sent by text or made by an app.
A nonprofit best known for the OWASP Top 10 list of web application risks.
A cloud provider runs the servers and operating system; you deploy only your app.
Controls, records and limits the use of administrator accounts.
The Linux and Unix framework that decides how logins are checked.

acronyms.full: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
acronyms.plain: Security rules for any organization that stores, processes or sends payment card data.
Each session gets its own key, so a server key stolen later can't decrypt past traffic.
Encrypts and signs email and files with public keys.
Health information that identifies a person, protected under HIPAA in the US.
Information that identifies a person, such as a name with a birth date, address or ID number.
The certificate authorities, certificates and rules that let people trust public keys.
A shared password set up in advance, like a home Wi-Fi password.
Software that isn't quite malware but is unwanted, such as adware or bundled toolbars.
Central login checks (AAA) for Wi-Fi, VPNs and network devices.
Malware that gives an attacker hidden remote control of a computer.
Access is granted by job role rather than person by person.
A flaw that lets an attacker run their own code on a system over the network.
Microsoft's protocol for controlling a Windows desktop remotely; keep it off the internet.
The most data, measured in time, you can afford to lose; it sets how often to back up.
A widely used public-key algorithm for encryption and signatures, named after its inventors.
How quickly a system must be working again after an outage.
Software you use over the internet while the provider runs everything, such as webmail.
An XML standard for single sign-on between an identity provider and apps.
Networking and security (VPN, firewall, web filtering) delivered together from the cloud.
A list of every component and library inside a piece of software.
Systems that monitor and control industrial equipment spread over a large area, such as pipelines.
The stages of building software, from planning and coding through testing, release and upkeep.
Network behavior set centrally in software instead of on each device.
A drive that encrypts everything written to it in its own hardware.
Encrypted file transfer over SSH; the safe replacement for FTP.
A family of hash functions; SHA-256 is common today, SHA-1 is no longer safe for signatures.
Collects and correlates logs from many systems to spot attacks and support investigations.
A contract that sets the service a provider promises, such as uptime or response times.
The cost of one incident: asset value times exposure factor (EF).
Windows file and printer sharing on port 445; keep it off the internet.
Encrypts and signs email using certificates.
Monitors and manages network devices; version 3 adds encryption and proper logins.
Automates repeatable security tasks and response playbooks across tools.
The team, and often the room, that monitors an organization's security around the clock.
Audit reports, such as SOC 2, showing how a service provider protects customer data.
A switch feature that copies traffic to another port so a monitoring tool can see it.
A DNS record listing which servers may send email for a domain.
One part whose failure stops the whole system.
Sneaking database commands into an app's input so the app runs them.
An encrypted remote command line, also used for file transfer (SFTP, SCP).
The old, insecure predecessor of TLS; the name lives on in the phrase SSL certificate.
One login gives access to many apps.
Tricks a server into making requests the attacker chooses, often to internal systems.
A standard format for describing and sharing threat intelligence.

acronyms.full: Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information
acronyms.plain: The protocol for sending and receiving STIX threat intelligence between organizations.
Encrypts traffic between two systems; it is what puts the S in HTTPS.
A code from an authenticator app that changes every 30 seconds or so.
A chip in a computer that stores keys and checks the boot process; used by BitLocker.
How an attacker operates, from goals down to specific steps; MITRE ATT&CK catalogs them.
Learns normal behavior of users and devices and flags activity that doesn't fit.
The firmware that starts a modern computer, replacing BIOS; it supports Secure Boot.
One appliance combining firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus and web filtering.
Splits one physical network into separate logical networks.
An encrypted tunnel across another network, such as the internet.
Filters web traffic to block attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
The current Wi-Fi security standard; it protects passwords better than WPA2.
A shortcut for joining Wi-Fi; its PIN method is weak and should be turned off.
Like EDR, but also pulls in data from email, network, cloud and identity tools.
Getting a website to run an attacker's script in other visitors' browsers.
Grants access to one app at a time after checking user and device, instead of a whole network.
